opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, the thing I'd most like to see is less boilerplate around the agent loop itself. Right now, if you want to build something that uses tools, you end up writing the same scaffolding every time: call the model, check whether it wants to use a tool, run that tool, append the result to the message history, call the model again, and repeat until it's done. It's not hard, but everybody rewrites it, and everybody makes slightly different mistakes, like how errors get passed back or what happens when the model calls several tools in parallel.

So I'd love for the SDK to handle that loop natively. You'd hand it your tools as plain functions, with the schema inferred from type hints and docstrings rather than hand-written JSON schema, and it would just run until the model has an answer. You'd still get hooks to step in, approve a dangerous action, or log what's happening, but the default path would be a few lines of code.

The second thing is making tool definitions easier to get right. A lot of what we learned building agents is that the tool interface matters as much as the prompt. Clear parameter names, good descriptions, examples of correct usage, and formats that are natural for the model to write. I think of it like designing an interface for a human junior engineer: if you'd have to explain it to a person, you need to explain it to the model too. So anything the SDK can do to nudge people toward well-documented tools, or flag ambiguous ones, would pay off a lot.

And the last piece is observability. When an agent goes off the rails, you want to see exactly what it saw and why it chose what it did. Better built-in tracing of tool calls and results would make iterating on these systems much faster.

r001.rationale: It proposes giving the SDK tools as plain functions and inferring their schemas from type hints and docstrings, which communicates passing function objects directly as tools.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, the biggest thing I'd want is for the SDK to get out of the way more. Right now a lot of the ergonomics are built around the idea that you, the developer, are going to carefully hand-write a JSON schema for every tool, pass it in, parse the tool_use block, run the thing, format a tool_result, and loop. That's fine when you have three tools. It gets painful when you have thirty, or when the tools are themselves dynamic.

So a few concrete things. First, I'd love it if defining a tool were basically just writing a function. Decorate a Python function, the SDK reads the type hints and the docstring, builds the schema, and handles the round-trip. We've all written that helper ourselves five times. It should just be there.

Second, the agent loop should be a first-class primitive, not something every team reinvents. Give me a `run` that takes a model, a set of tools, and a stopping condition, and handles the while loop, the streaming, the retries, and the error handling. And make it easy to inject myself in the middle, because the interesting work is always in the middle: logging, approvals, modifying tool results before the model sees them, cutting off a runaway loop.

Third, better support for what actually happens in long-running agents. Context grows. Tool results get huge. You want to truncate, summarize, or swap things out of the window, and today that's all on you. The SDK knows the token counts and the structure of the conversation better than I do, so it should help.

And then the one I care about most from the research side: I want the SDK to make the model's job easier, not just mine. A lot of tool-use failures aren't the model being dumb, they're the tool being badly described or the result being formatted in a way that's confusing. So I'd like built-in nudges toward good tool design. Tell me when my description is ambiguous. Tell me when two tools overlap. Give me a quick harness to test whether the model picks the right tool across a set of prompts. That kind of feedback loop would raise the floor for everyone building on it.

The theme in all of this is that the model is getting more capable, and the SDK should shift from being a thin wrapper around an HTTP call to being the thing that encodes everything we've learned about how to let a model use tools well.

r001.rationale: The response proposes defining a tool by writing and decorating a Python function, which the SDK would use to build the schema and handle the round-trip.

astra-6.text: I’d love for the SDK to handle more of the boilerplate around tool use. Ideally, I could pass in a Python function, have it infer the tool schema from the types and docstring, and let it handle calling the function and returning the result to the model. You’d still want control over execution, especially for anything with side effects, but the simple case should be really simple.

r001.rationale: The response explicitly proposes passing a Python function into the SDK as a tool.

sol-6.1.text: I’d love for it to handle more of the tool-use loop for you. You should be able to pass in a Python function, have the SDK generate the schema, and then have it execute the function when the model calls it and send the result back. You’d still want access to the individual steps, but the basic case should take very little code.

r001.rationale: The response says users should be able to pass a Python function to the SDK, which would generate its schema and execute it when called by the model.
